--- title: "Pure-Premium Tutorial" --- We estimate the expected claim cost per year of cover for a policy: its pure premium. We compare two approaches, predicted frequency multiplied by predicted average claim amount, and a direct Tweedie prediction. Fitting both with GLUM and LightGBM gives four estimates for the same test policies. If you are new to pricing models, start with the [targets and weights](index.qmd#targets-and-weights), then read in order. We prepare and split the data, explore uncapped training outcomes, select Tweedie power, fit GLUM, check its working distributions, fit LightGBM, and evaluate the four estimates. The collapsed “Look inside” notes explain the mathematics and library functions in more detail. If you already fit pricing models, use the [conditional diagnostics](#sec-conditional-diagnostics) to review the distribution assumptions, then follow the [test audit](#sec-test-audit) through accuracy, calibration, and ranking to the [recorded findings](#sec-test-findings). Run the Python cells in order, whichever reading path you choose. Each portfolio average divides a total by the volume over which it was observed: - Frequency is total claim count divided by total exposure, or the exposure-weighted mean of policy frequencies. - Severity is total capped claim amount divided by total claim count, or the claim-count-weighted mean of severity among claim-bearing policies. - Pure premium is total capped claim amount divided by total exposure, or the exposure-weighted mean of policy pure premiums. The cell checks the frequency and pure-premium identities: ::: {#fe399933 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} avg_frequency = splits.train["ClaimNb"].sum() / splits.train["Exposure"].sum() avg_frequency_check = np.average(splits.train["Frequency"], weights=splits.train["Exposure"]) avg_pure_premium = splits.train["ClaimAmountCapped"].sum() / splits.train["Exposure"].sum() avg_pure_premium_check = np.average(splits.train["PurePremium"], weights=splits.train["Exposure"]) print(f"Average frequency: {avg_frequency:.6f} claim / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_frequency_check:.6f}") print(f"Average pure premium: {avg_pure_premium:.2f} EUR / year") print(f" check (weighted mean of rate): {avg_pure_premium_check:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average frequency: 0.073705 claim / year check (weighted mean of rate): 0.073705 Average pure premium: 137.57 EUR / year check (weighted mean of rate): 137.57 ``` ::: ::: Multiplying a target by its weight recovers the policy's claim count for frequency, or its capped claim amount for severity and pure premium. `portfolio_calibration_table` and `evaluate_predictions` use this identity to compare observed and predicted totals. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Look inside: `TARGET_SPECS` and `target_and_weight` `TARGET_SPECS` defines each component's target, weight, and eligible rows. `target_and_weight` looks up that definition and returns `(rows, target_array, weight_array)`. Use every training policy, accounting for unequal exposures and claim counts. Severity here is uncapped; the capped modelling targets remain unchanged. Tail disagreement can expose limitations of a reference. Pooled agreement cannot establish conditional model validity or select a model family. Here we estimate a shared portfolio mean and, for severity, Gamma dispersion. The means do not vary with policy characteristics. The later [conditional diagnostics](#sec-conditional-diagnostics) repeat the comparison using means predicted from those characteristics by the fitted GLUM models. ### Frequency with unequal exposures The constant annual rate $\hat\lambda$ is total claims divided by total exposure. Compare exposure-weighted count proportions with the same weighted mixture of Poisson distributions, each with mean $e_i\hat\lambda$, where $e_i$ is policy $i$'s exposure in years. A Poisson at the annual rate alone would treat every policy as a full year. Keep zero claims and a final overflow bin, so both probability distributions sum to one. Pooling policies with different exposures or risks can make the count variance exceed the count mean, even if each policy follows a Poisson distribution at its own mean. The policy average becomes less variable as its claim count grows under the Gamma assumption below. Both plotted distributions use claim-count weights. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Why claim count changes the Gamma reference Under independent Gamma claims with a common mean $\mu$ and dispersion $\phi$, the policy average $y_i$ has shape $n_i/\phi$, scale $\phi\mu/n_i$, and variance $\phi\mu^2/n_i$. Each policy contributes once to the fitting likelihood; its claim count already enters through the shape and scale. ::: ::: {#exploratory-severity-reference .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} uncapped_severity_rows = splits.train.loc[splits.train["ClaimNb"] > 0].copy() uncapped_severity_rows["UncappedSeverity"] = ( uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimAmountOriginal"] / uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimNb"] ) uncapped_y = uncapped_severity_rows["UncappedSeverity"].to_numpy(dtype=float) uncapped_n = uncapped_severity_rows["ClaimNb"].to_numpy(dtype=float) uncapped_mean = np.average(uncapped_y, weights=uncapped_n) uncapped_phi = fit_gamma_dispersion( uncapped_y, np.full_like(uncapped_y, uncapped_mean), uncapped_n ) mixture_counts, mixture_policies = np.unique(uncapped_n, return_counts=True) mixture_weights = mixture_counts * mixture_policies / uncapped_n.sum() severity_grid = np.geomspace(uncapped_y.min(), uncapped_y.max(), 512) severity_shape = mixture_counts / uncapped_phi severity_scale = uncapped_phi * uncapped_mean / mixture_counts severity_density = gamma.pdf( severity_grid[:, None], a=severity_shape, scale=severity_scale ) @ mixture_weights severity_survival = gamma.sf( severity_grid[:, None], a=severity_shape, scale=severity_scale ) @ mixture_weights severity_x, severity_empirical_sf = weighted_empirical_ccdf(uncapped_y, uncapped_n) print( f"All {len(uncapped_y):,} claim-bearing training policies; {int(uncapped_n.sum()):,} claims; " f"uncapped mean={uncapped_mean:,.2f} EUR; base phi={uncapped_phi:.6g}; " f"maximum policy average={uncapped_y.max():,.2f} EUR" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All 19,955 claim-bearing training policies; 21,146 claims; uncapped mean=2,346.72 EUR; base phi=1.54079; maximum policy average=4,075,400.56 EUR ``` ::: ::: The histogram uses logarithmic amount bins with density per euro. Below, $f_p$ is the Tweedie density for positive rates and its probability mass for zero. The mean $\hat\mu_i$ comes from the fitted model; $e_i$ is exposure and $\phi$ is base dispersion. The validation log likelihood is $$ L(p,\phi)=\sum_i \log f_p(y_i;\hat\mu_i,\phi/e_i), \qquad y_i=\frac{\text{ClaimAmountCapped}_i}{e_i}. $$ `fit_tweedie_dispersion` optimizes $\log\phi$. The Pearson estimate $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2/\hat\mu_i^p$ supplies only the starting value; a failed optimization raises. `tweedie_log_likelihood` uses [GLUM's scalar-dispersion density API](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/glm.html#glum.TweedieDistribution.log_likelihood) with $a_i=e_i^{1/(2-p)}$, transformed observations $a_i y_i$, transformed means $a_i\hat\mu_i$, and unit likelihood weights. It adds the Jacobian $\sum_{y_i>0}\log a_i$ for positive rates. Zero claims retain their probability mass, with no Jacobian term. Targets and weights follow the [GLUM motor tutorial](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/glm_french_motor_tutorial/glm_french_motor.html). ::: {#19a928b8 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_source(select_tweedie_power) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} ```python def select_tweedie_power( development_train: pd.DataFrame, development_validation: pd.DataFrame, powers: tuple[float, ...] = TWEEDIE_POWERS, ) -> tuple[float, pd.DataFrame]: """Select p by validation profile likelihood under the fitted rate convention.""" train_rows, y_train, w_train = target_and_weight(development_train, "pure_premium") validation_rows, y_validation, w_validation = target_and_weight( development_validation, "pure_premium" ) results = [] for power in powers: family = TweedieDistribution(power) model = GeneralizedLinearRegressor( family=family, link="log", formula=RATING_FORMULA, drop_first=True, alpha=0, max_iter=200, ).fit(train_rows, y_train, sample_weight=w_train) train_prediction = model.predict(train_rows) validation_prediction = model.predict(validation_rows) dispersion = fit_tweedie_dispersion(y_train, train_prediction, w_train, power) log_likelihood = tweedie_log_likelihood( y_validation, validation_prediction, w_validation, power, dispersion ) results.append( { "power": power, "training_dispersion": dispersion, "validation_log_likelihood": log_likelihood, } ) profile = pd.DataFrame(results) if not np.isfinite(profile["validation_log_likelihood"]).all(): raise RuntimeError("Tweedie profile likelihood produced non-finite values") selected = float( profile.loc[profile["validation_log_likelihood"].idxmax(), "power"] ) return selected, profile ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Fit an interpretable GLUM benchmark {#sec-glum-benchmark} The GLUM benchmark lets us judge whether a flexible model earns its extra complexity. Fit a regularized model, which penalizes coefficient size, for prediction. Fit a separate unregularized model for coefficient intervals, categorical relativities (multiplicative effects on the predicted rate), and sandwich standard errors, which allow the variance to differ from the working distribution. For each categorical term, the relativity compares that level with the omitted reference level while holding other predictors fixed. The intercept, continuous terms, and individual spline coefficients keep their coefficient intervals but have blank relativity cells. Comparing two ages requires combining all spline coefficients with the difference between the spline basis values at those ages, then exponentiating that combined log-rate change. An individual spline coefficient is not an age relativity. The table recognizes main-effect treatment terms named `C()[...]` for `VehBrand`, `VehPower`, `VehGas`, `Region`, and `Area`. This rule must be reviewed if the formula adds interactions or uses different contrast coding. The unregularized model's confidence intervals describe that fit. They do not apply to the penalized predictive fit. Review relativities for plausibility and choose predictions using out-of-sample evidence. Exposure and claim count determine each policy's weight in fitting. The standard-error calculation also needs the number of independent policy rows. GLUM 3.4.1 uses total weight in its small-sample adjustment, so we calculate covariance with a copy of the weights rescaled to average one. This preserves their relative values and the fitted means, while making the adjustment use the number of policy rows. Original exposures and claim counts still define the targets, totals, and distribution parameters. This inference assumes independence between policy rows. We set dispersion to one only for the sandwich calculation: its common scalar cancels between the information matrix and score contributions. The fitted distribution dispersions remain separate. `fit_glum_predictive` uses 3-fold cross-validation to compare penalty strengths $\alpha$ and penalty mixtures $\mathrm{l1\_ratio}$ (0 for ridge, 1 for lasso). Here the [GLUM models](#sec-glum-benchmark) supply means that vary with policy characteristics. A conditional distribution describes variation in outcomes at a given policy's predicted mean, exposure, and claim count where applicable. The table lists the working references for each component, using the capped modelling targets. The survival curves compare upper tails, the zero-mass table compares the probabilities of no claims and no loss, and the Pearson residual check compares squared errors scaled by the assumed variance. Empirical and reference curves use matching weights: exposure for counts and policy totals, claim count for severity. Their sum is called risk volume. Agreement in these pooled training views cannot establish correctness for each policy or performance on the test set. Here $e_i$ is policy exposure, $n_i$ is claim count, $\hat\lambda_i$ is predicted annual frequency, and $\hat\mu_i$ is predicted severity or pure premium, according to the row. Base dispersion $\phi$ controls variance before adjustment for claim count or exposure; $p$ is the selected Tweedie variance power. | Observable | Conditional reference | Curve weight | | --- | --- | --- | | Policy claim count | Poisson mean $e_i\hat\lambda_i$ | Exposure $e_i$ | | Positive capped policy-average severity | Gamma shape $n_i/\phi$, scale $\phi\hat\mu_i/n_i$ | Claim count $n_i$ | | Capped policy total | Tweedie mean $e_i\hat\mu_i$, dispersion $\phi e_i^{1-p}$ | Exposure $e_i$ | ### Fit dispersion parameters; means stay fixed Keep the GLUM predicted rates fixed. Estimate Gamma base dispersion for severity, Tweedie base dispersion for pure premium, and Negative Binomial shape for frequency on every eligible training row. The Poisson reference needs only the predicted policy count, so it has no additional parameter to fit. The Negative Binomial (NB2) form used here has variance $m_i+m_i^2/r$, where $m_i=e_i\hat\lambda_i$ is the predicted policy count and $r$ is the shape parameter. Smaller $r$ allows more variation; as $r$ grows, the reference approaches Poisson, whose variance is $m_i$. This NB overlay is a dispersion diagnostic; the fitted frequency pricing model remains Poisson. After those fits finish, sample up to 20,000 policies per component with seed 42 and reuse each component's rows, predictions, and weights throughout. ::: {#fit-diagnostic-parameters .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} training_rows = {} training_predictions = {} for component in TARGET_SPECS: rows, _, _ = target_and_weight(splits.train, component) training_rows[component] = rows training_predictions[component] = pd.Series( glum_models[component].predict(rows), index=rows.index, dtype=float ) severity_train = training_rows["severity"] gamma_dispersion = fit_gamma_dispersion( severity_train["Severity"], training_predictions["severity"], severity_train["ClaimNb"], ) nb_shape = fit_negative_binomial_shape( training_rows["frequency"]["ClaimNb"], training_rows["frequency"]["Exposure"] * training_predictions["frequency"], ) tweedie_dispersion = fit_tweedie_dispersion( training_rows["pure_premium"]["PurePremium"], training_predictions["pure_premium"], training_rows["pure_premium"]["Exposure"], selected_power, ) dispersions = {"frequency": 1.0, "severity": gamma_dispersion, "pure_premium": tweedie_dispersion} ``` ::: ::: {#cell-sample-diagnostic-policies .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} diagnostic_rows = {} diagnostic_predictions = {} for component, rows in training_rows.items(): sample = rows.sample(n=min(20_000, len(rows)), random_state=42) diagnostic_rows[component] = sample diagnostic_predictions[component] = training_predictions[component].loc[sample.index] print_frame( "Training diagnostic scope", pd.DataFrame({ "eligible_training_policies": {name: len(rows) for name, rows in training_rows.items()}, "plotted_policies": {name: len(rows) for name, rows in diagnostic_rows.items()}, "base_dispersion": dispersions, }), ) print(f"NB shape: {nb_shape:.6g} (infinity denotes the Poisson limit)") ``` ::: {#sample-diagnostic-policies .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
